question: According to multiple investigative reports, including reports by Fox News Digital, fourteen leading US environmental organisations advocating for stricter climate laws have reportedly received over USD 497 million in 2023 from Energy Foundation China (EFC), a Beijingbased organisation with documented links to Chinese state institutions and the Chinese Communist Party1.

EFC publicly promotes ‘energy cooperation’ between China and the West2 and has previously funded international NGOs that are also active in Europe. These findings raise concerns that Chinese state-linked foundations may be shaping environmental and energy policies within the EU.

In its reply to Priority Question for Written Answer P-10-2025-0032373, the Commission acknowledged the existence of government-organised non-governmental organisations (GONGOs) but confirmed that it does not regularly monitor or classify them. In this context, I ask the Commission: 1.

Given that the Commission does not monitor GONGOs, how does it ensure that foreign state-linked entities such as EFC do not influence EU climate and energy policymaking, directly or indirectly, through European NGOs?
Does the Commission plan to establish a screening or transparency mechanism to identify and exclude foreign GONGOs from participation in EU consultations or funding schemes?
Will the Commission re-evaluate existing partnerships with environmental NGOs that receive funding from foreign state-affiliated foundations in order to safeguard EU policy independence?

Fox News Digital, ‘CCP-tied group is quietly fueling US-based climate initiatives’, December 2023, https://www.foxnews.com/politics/ccp-tied-group-quietly-fueling-us-based-climate-initiatives-tax-filings. Energy Foundation China, ‘About Us’, https://www.efchina.org/About-Us-en/Introduction-en. https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/P-10-2025-003237_EN.html.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.1.2026) The Commission is committed to transparency in its relations with interest representatives, including non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and other stakeholders. Interest representatives carrying out activities to influence EU policy or legislation must register in the Transparency Register, irrespective of their country of establishment.

The Commission requires prior registration for any related meetings with its decision-makers at political and administrative level or for participating in Commission expert groups. EU and third-country NGOs are required to provide in the register the information, including financial information, set out in Annex II to the applicable Interinstitutional Agreement1.

To increase the transparency and democratic accountability of activities impacting EU decision-making processes, the Commission also adopted in 2023 its proposal for a Directive on interest representation on behalf of third countries. The proposed harmonised transparency requirements would apply to entities carrying out interest representation on behalf of third countries, regardless of their legal form.

The proposal is currently being discussed by the colegislators. The Commission exercises the necessary scrutiny and due diligence when selecting NGOs with which it partners in the use of EU funds. The Financial Regulation includes a definition of NGO to ensure the reliability and transparency of information in the Financial Transparency System, where information on recipients is available.

In the event of incorrect implementation or in cases of fraud, irregularities, substantial errors or serious breach of contractual obligations, including the violation of EU values, the grant may be suspended, terminated or reduced and funds may be recovered.
